title: Our Father, once more
hook: the prayer from the first week, now with five years in it
tomorrow: which word did a whole crowd shout with their hands in the air?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voices: a child's chant over a garden wall, all shall be well, a burden rolling away. Their words, your road.

Journal pages fill up with I: I need, I'm sorry, I hope. Now count the I's in the prayer this path met in its first week. In Matthew, in the King James, it says our, us, we. Not once does it say I, me or my. Pray it alone in an empty room and it still won't let you go singular. So whose Father is this?
screen: `I NEED, I'M SORRY, I HOPE.` → `ZERO I'S.` → `WHOSE FATHER?`

segments.voice: Here's how Matthew gives the opening: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." In the first week these were new words. Now there are five years in them, and the first one holds the rest. Our. The prophet Malachi asked it long before: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" One father, one family, and his very next question is why people deal falsely with their own brothers. Christians differ on how wide that our reaches, but the prayer itself never shrinks to my. Now a neighbor who says it too. In the Days of Awe, around the Jewish new year and Yom Kippur, Jewish prayer repeats Avinu Malkeinu, our Father, our King, line after line asking for mercy. Two traditions, one word in common: our Father. And an honest difference. Christians pray the Lord's Prayer as the prayer Jesus taught, the one they call God's Son; Jews don't pray it as his prayer or share that belief about him, and Avinu Malkeinu has its own words and its own season. Neither is a copy of the other. Both say our. Churches pray this one in different ways too: some end with For thine is the kingdom, some say trespasses for debts, some sing it. The words barely change. The people saying them do.
screen: `NOT ONCE: I, ME, MY.` · `HAVE WE NOT ALL ONE FATHER?` · `AVINU MALKEINU: OUR FATHER, OUR KING.` · `SHARED WORD, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `OUR FATHER.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer slowly, one line to a breath, and stop wherever a word holds you. If you don't, let the words pass through your mind and count each us and our.
Our Father. The prayer from the first week, word for word the same, with five years now folded into its first word.
The line for today: our father, never my father in this prayer. Sleep well, or good morning.

fork.setup: your Jewish neighbor says her family prays "our Father, our King" at the new year. what's a fair reply?
options: "so it's the same prayer as ours, just in Hebrew."
"we both call God our Father; ours is the prayer Jesus taught."
"then your family should pray the Lord's Prayer too."
fork.reveal: Avinu Malkeinu and the Lord's Prayer share the words our Father. they're different prayers from different seasons, and neither is a copy of the other: shared ground, honest difference.

chat.says: nia asked if the "our" in our father includes her. her family doesn't believe in God. help??
options: Tell her it never says 'my.' Malachi asks, have we not all one father? That's how I hear it.
Tell her no. The 'our' only means the people who already pray it in church.
Tell her it doesn't matter, since every religion's prayers mean exactly the same thing.
chat.meaning: The Lord's Prayer says us and our, never I or my, and Malachi asks, 'Have we not all one father?' Christians differ on how wide the 'our' reaches.

Days of Awe.meaning: the Jewish holy days from the new year to Yom Kippur

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: wisdom: whose Father is this? The prayer's 'our', Malachi 2:10, and the unity thread). Title, word, carry kept; Malachi 2:10 and Avinu Malkeinu added; the doxology is now mentioned only as a church variant (Matthew 6:13 no longer quoted).

Unity thread (weekly neighbor): Judaism. Avinu Malkeinu ('our Father, our King') is paraphrased with no quotation, cited to the High Holy Day liturgy. 'Around the Jewish new year and Yom Kippur… line after line asking for mercy' describes its use in the Days of Awe; customs differ (e.g. some communities omit it on Shabbat). Honest difference stated: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer as the prayer Jesus taught, whom they call God's Son; Jews don't pray it as his prayer or share that belief. Please have a Jewish reviewer confirm this is fair and accurate, and that nothing implies the two prayers are the same or that one copies the other.

Malachi 2:10 quoted from the KJV; 'deal falsely with their own brothers' paraphrases the verse's next clause ('deal treacherously every man against his brother'). 'Christians differ on how wide that our reaches' is hedged, no counts. Confirm.
'Not once does it say I, me or my' is checked against the KJV text of Matthew 6:9–13. Please confirm.
